text: Let's compare. The same water to start. The same time. The same air and wind. Only the water temperature is different. Which loses more: warmer water or cooler water? Make a guess.
The warmer water loses more. It evaporates faster. Both can evaporate. This is a simple model, not a measurement.
Try all four pairs. Keep your results. What is missing when the ice cannot grow?
A drop of water. A big adventure. Listen, try, and look closely.
Look at the puddle. There is water on the ground. Tap the sun button below. Let time pass.
There is less water now. Where did the water go? Make a guess. Then tap the magnifying glass.
Some water goes into the air. It becomes water vapor. We cannot see water vapor. The dots are a model. Water can evaporate without boiling.
There is water vapor in the air. We cannot see it. Cool this wet air. Tap the snowflake.
Some water vapor becomes tiny drops. This is condensation. Many tiny drops make a cloud. Cold clouds can have ice crystals, too. This is a close-up model. A cloud does not always make rain.
Look inside the cloud. The drops are tiny. Tap the two drops. Make them join.
The drops get bigger. Make them join again.
The drops grow. Now they can fall from the cloud. They reach the ground as rain. This is a fast, close-up model.
In a very cold cloud, water vapor can become ice crystals. They grow into snowflakes. Will they reach the ground as snow? Choose the air below.
The air stays cold. The snow does not melt away. Snow reaches the ground. Now try the warm air.
The snow falls through a thick warm layer. It melts into drops. Rain reaches the ground. Snow does not start as frozen raindrops. Now try the cold air.
This is a tall storm cloud. Here is a small piece of ice. Add a strong updraft. Add supercooled drops. The drops are below zero, but still liquid.
The updraft is ready. It holds the ice up in the cloud.
The supercooled drops are ready. They can freeze onto the ice.
Turn on both the updraft and the cold drops. Then tap the play button.
Both are ready. Tap the play button below. Watch the ice.
The updraft holds the ice up. Drops freeze onto it. Hail grows in layers. It falls when the air cannot hold it up. This is a fast, close-up model.
Water is back on the ground. It can take different paths. Choose a river, the soil, or a lake. Try each path.
Some water flows over the ground. It joins a stream. It can reach a lake or the sea. Melting snow can take this path, too.
Some water soaks into the soil. It fills spaces in soil and rock. Groundwater can move slowly to a stream.
Some water stays in a lake. Later, it may evaporate or flow away. Drops can take different paths.

Water can take many paths. It evaporates. It condenses into tiny cloud drops. Growing drops fall as rain. Snow can melt on the way down. Hail needs an updraft and supercooled drops. Water flows, soaks in, or stays. Choose a stop and try again.
